name: Latanoprost

lead: Latanoprost is a prescription eye drop for glaucoma and raised eye pressure. Its label lists longer, thicker, darker eyelashes and darker eyelid skin and irises among its effects.
Looksmaxxing discussion is sparse and mostly about eye darkening. No trial has tested it for cosmetic purposes; a Phase 1/2 trial pairing it with laser in alopecia areata is registered.

paras: It is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue that increases fluid drainage from the eye through the uveoscleral pathway, lowering pressure. Pigment and lash changes are tissue effects of the same drug class.

Label warnings include permanent iris pigmentation, eyelid darkening, inflammation and macular oedema. A case report describes skin depigmentation. It is prescription-only and not approved for cosmetic use.

forums.title: Latanoprost can make your eyes darker

lead: Latanoprost is a synthetic prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue applied as an ophthalmic solution to lower raised intraocular pressure (IOP) in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. The US label describes its main action as increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour.[1][2] It is a prescription medicine, and its approved use is medical rather than cosmetic.

Its relevance to appearance comes from side effects listed on its label: increased length, thickness, pigmentation and number of eyelashes, darkening of eyelid skin, and permanent darkening of the iris.[1] Related prostaglandin analogues, notably bimatoprost, have been developed specifically for eyelash growth, and latanoprost is discussed by some users in the same context. A registered Phase 1/2 trial has also listed latanoprost combined with fractional laser for alopecia areata.[3]

No published trial in the sources reviewed tests latanoprost as a cosmetic eyelash or eye-colour treatment. Evidence for its eyelash effect comes from its glaucoma trials and label, and community discussion of eye darkening is largely anecdotal and often framed as a curiosity.
infobox: Raised intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma / ocular hypertension

paras: The US label indicates latanoprost 0.005% for reducing elevated IOP in patients with open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension.[1] Early six-month randomised trials compared once-daily latanoprost with twice-daily timolol in several countries and found it lowered pressure at least as well, with the advantage of once-daily dosing.[4][5][6] A meta-analysis of randomised trials of common glaucoma drugs and a later network meta-analysis of first-line agents both include prostaglandin analogues among the most effective topical options.[7][8] The UK Glaucoma Treatment Study, a placebo-controlled trial, reported visual-field preservation with latanoprost in newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma.[9]

Eyelash lengthening and thickening is a recognised effect of latanoprost and other prostaglandin analogues; the label states the changes are usually reversible.[1] Eyelash growth has also been noted as a common mild adverse event of the related drug travoprost.[10] Latanoprost is not approved for eyelash enhancement, and it is not the product marketed for that purpose.

A looksmax.org thread discusses latanoprost, bimatoprost and travoprost as agents that can darken eye colour; its author described the idea as of limited usefulness and risky because the drugs are glaucoma treatments, and asked that it not be taken too seriously.[11] The label states that iris pigmentation is likely to be permanent.[1]

The US label lists iris pigmentation changes, eyelid skin darkening, eyelash changes, intraocular inflammation (iritis/uveitis) and macular oedema, including cystoid macular oedema, among reported reactions. It says pigmentation can increase for as long as treatment continues, and that iris pigmentation is likely to be permanent while eyelash changes are usually reversible.[1] Grokipedia adds that iris changes are more pronounced in people with mixed-colour irises, and lists conjunctival hyperaemia as a common effect.[12]

A published case report describes skin depigmentation associated with latanoprost use.[13] The label notes that no adequate well-controlled studies exist in pregnant women and that animal studies using intravenous dosing showed malformations and embryofetal loss.[1]

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue and FP receptor agonist. The label says its main mechanism, from animal and human studies, is increased uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour.[1] Reviews of prostaglandin mechanisms describe tissue remodelling in the outflow pathways as part of the effect.[14] Small clinical studies have also measured effects on choroidal thickness.[15][16]

Human studies are overwhelmingly in glaucoma and ocular hypertension. Large randomised trials from the 1990s (US, Scandinavian and UK groups) compared latanoprost with timolol over six months,[4][5][6] and a two-year analysis and a one-year combination trial with timolol followed.[17][18] Head-to-head trials compared it with bimatoprost and travoprost.[19][20][21]

No published trial of latanoprost for cosmetic eyelash enhancement or eye-colour change was identified. The one registered trial related to hair is a Phase 1/2 study (n=70, start 2024, status unknown) of latanoprost combined with fractional erbium-YAG laser in alopecia areata.[3] A systematic review of androgenetic alopecia treatments does not establish latanoprost as a treatment in that condition.[22]

Latanoprost is a prescription medicine. In looksmaxxing forums it appears mainly in passing, as a drug whose documented side effects touch on eye colour and lashes; the single source list thread frames it as curiosity rather than a protocol, and replies were joking about eye colour preferences.[11]

lore.intro: Latanoprost is a minor topic in appearance communities, mentioned chiefly for its eye-darkening side effect.[11]

claims.claim: Prostaglandin drops such as latanoprost can make eyes darker
